[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): We will take it step by step. Since when have you been this tired?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): That I cannot date, doctor. Maybe a few months, maybe it started along with the periods last year, I truly don't remember. Even after sleeping the whole night I feel drained, and if I stand up quickly I feel giddy. Will I faint one day?
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you actually fainted?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I have not fainted. It is only a light feeling, then it passes.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the breathlessness, when does that come on?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): When I climb to our flat, it is the second floor, or if I walk fast for the bus. Sitting quietly I am fine. Doctor, is my heart becoming weak?
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): I would not call the heart weak from the story alone. Any chest pain along with the breathlessness?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no chest pain at all.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any swelling in the feet, or palpitations, the heart racing?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Feet are not swollen. Um, sometimes the heart beats fast when I am very tired... well, actually, no, I would not call it palpitations. It is more just the exhaustion.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, we will leave palpitations aside. Tell me about the periods in ordinary words, how heavy they are.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): They are very heavy since one year. I go through so many pads that I lose count, many in a day, and there are big clots, quite big, though I cannot say the size. Could it be a tumour inside?
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): I am not calling it a tumour from this chair. How many days does the bleeding last now?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Seven or eight days, and sometimes it drags on even more. Earlier it used to finish in four days only.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you get pain or cramps with it?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, cramps on the first two days. I take Crocin for that, the pain-and-fever tablet, one tablet when the cramp comes. If I take it every month, will my kidneys get spoiled?
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Crocin is paracetamol, and one tablet for the cramp, within what the strip says, is generally safe for the kidneys. Are you on any other tablets?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): The red iron tablets, for the blood. I take them sometimes only, when I remember, not daily. A neighbour said they cause constipation, so I skip them. Is that the reason I am still so weak?
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): The nurse read your medication list just now, and she has put down ferrous sulphate 200 mg twice a day.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No, that is not right. I never take it twice. I think the tablet is 100 mg, the small red one, but I am not sure of the number. Has she mixed my paper with another patient's?
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): We should not settle the strength from memory. Kindly bring the strip when you come next. Separately, have you noticed hair fall?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, a lot of hair comes away in the shower, since some months. My mother says thyroid is there in our family, her sister is taking thyroid tablets. Do you think I also have thyroid, and is that why the hair is falling?
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): I will note thyroid disease in your mother's sister. Has your weight gone up or down?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No, the weight is the same, as far as I know. I have not checked on a scale.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): How are the bowels, and passing urine?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Motions are normal. There is no burning when I pass urine. I am vegetarian, doctor, I hardly eat any greens, and at the bank I sit the whole day. Can a poor diet make the blood this low?
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): A low-greens diet can contribute, yes. Do you smoke, or take any alcohol?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Never smoked, and I don't take alcohol. Am I troubling you with all these small questions?
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not at all, it helps. Any operation in the past, or diabetes, or high blood pressure?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No operation ever. No diabetes and no high BP. I was quite alright until these periods became heavy.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me examine you now. Pulse is 96 per minute, and the blood pressure is 108 over 70. Your palms are pale, the ankles are not swollen, and the chest is clear with no wheeze.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Is 108 over 70 too low for me? Will I collapse on the stairs going home? And 96 for the pulse, is that a danger sign?
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): 108 over 70 is an acceptable pressure, not a collapse figure. A pulse of 96 can fit with the blood being a bit low. I am not finding fluid in the ankles or any wheeze.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): So you do think the blood is low. Please say it straight, will I need a blood transfusion? I am really frightened of transfusion.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): No transfusion is being planned. My working impression is iron deficiency from the heavy periods over this past year, and that would join up the tiredness, the breathlessness on climbing, the pale palms, and the hair fall.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Then what about the thyroid my mother spoke of? You have not really answered that, and I keep fearing it is something very bad.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thyroid disease remains on the differential, and I cannot rule it out today. The tests will tell us more than I can by talking.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): What tests, exactly? Will there be many needles, because I get very shaky? My cousin had a scan and then an operation for fibroids, are you going to do that to me?
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): I am arranging a full blood count, a ferritin level, and a thyroid function test, all from a single draw. No operation is arranged. We might do a pelvic ultrasound only if the bleeding is still this heavy once those results are back, and it is not booked today.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Should I take the red iron tablets every day from tonight? Is it 100 mg or the 200 mg the nurse read? I don't want to take a wrong dose and harm myself.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Please do not change the iron until you bring the strip and we have the ferritin. One Crocin when the cramp comes is fine. If you get more breathless, or chest pain, or you feel you are about to faint, come back sooner and do not wait out the week.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): If I stay much the same, when do I see you? Can I keep working at the bank, or should I take leave? And what should I be eating?
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in one week, and bring the reports plus the iron strip. You can continue at the bank, only don't rush for the bus. Try to take some green vegetables on most days.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): One week feels very long if this is serious. If a report is very bad, will somebody call me, or do I only find out here?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): If a result needs urgent action, we will contact you. Otherwise we sit with the numbers together in one week. Let me summarise it back, so we are not missing anything.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heavy periods for a year, with more pads than you can count and clots you cannot size, tiredness you cannot put a date on, breathlessness on the stairs but not while sitting, no chest pain, no fainting, no swollen feet. Hair fall for some months, red iron tablets only sometimes, which you say is not the nurse's ferrous sulphate 200 mg twice a day, and your mother's sister has thyroid disease. Blood tests today, a pelvic scan only if the bleeding stays this heavy after the results, and I will see you in one week.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that is all correct. I will bring the strip. If the thyroid test is normal, doctor, will my hair grow back?
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hair often improves once the cause is treated, but I will not promise regrowth before the results. We will go over everything in one week.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning. Come on through, both of you, and have a seat. What can I do for you today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Bit of a waste of your time, if I'm honest. It's just the toe.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Just the toe, he says. He was awake half the—
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I was not awake half the night. I dozed. Right big toe's a bit swollen, that's all. Came on yesterday afternoon.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yesterday afternoon, was it?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, scratch that. I was fine in the afternoon. It was last night, once I got into bed. Started throbbing then.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): And if you had to put a word to it?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): A niggle. Three out of ten, if you want a number. I walked in, didn't I?
[SEG0009] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He couldn't get his trainer on this morning. He was hanging off the kitchen doorframe, so don't let him—
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright. It kept me up. There, I've said it. Still hardly an emergency.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which foot?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. The big toe. Left one's got nothing to do with it.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): When you look at it, is it red, or hot?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Hot, a bit, yeah. I haven't studied it. She says it's red.
[SEG0015] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Bright red and shiny, right over the joint. You can see it from the doorway.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chance you injured it? Stubbed it, kicked something?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. I haven't done anything to it.
[SEG0018] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The chair in the—
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, yeah, I know. Dining chair, last night, in the hall. I did kick it, I'd forgotten. Mind you, the toe was already going before that... no, I've got it backwards. The kick was first, then it swelled up in bed.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Has the same thing ever happened before?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, I was going to say no, but there was that time...
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): A year back. Same big toe. Went down in a few days on its own, so I didn't bother coming in.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about medicines? Anything you take regularly, even if it doesn't feel related?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. I'm not one for pills. There's only the...
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Water tablet. Bendroflumethiazide. Five milligrams — no, two point five milligrams. One every morning, for the blood pressure. Been years.
[SEG0026] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And he does take that one. Every morning. I see him do it.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): And alcohol? I'm not going to lecture you, I just need the picture.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Weekends. A couple of beers. Saturday, sometimes the Sunday as well. Not in the week.
[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Both days, and it's more than a couple. He's right about the weeknights, though.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever with this, or do you feel unwell in yourself?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No temperature. I'm right as rain apart from the toe being a nuisance.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anywhere else sore? Another toe, an ankle, a knee?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Just this one. Nowhere else.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's have a look. Shoe and sock off for me. The right big toe joint is swollen, red and warm, and it's very tender as soon as I press it. The skin's intact, and the rest of the foot looks normal.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Very tender is pushing it. A bit sensitive, that's all.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're welcome to play it down. My working impression is a gout flare in that joint. The episode a year back was probably the same thing. I wouldn't call it confirmed, not before a blood test.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Gout? That's old men and port, isn't it. Feels like a lot of drama for one toe.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Weekend beer can set it off, and a water tablet like yours can push the uric acid up. I'll request a blood test for uric acid, and kidney function on the same sample, seeing as you're on the bendroflumethiazide.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): It'll have gone before you get the result. Still, if you reckon it's worth it.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): For the pain I'm prescribing colchicine. I nearly wrote one milligram twice a day, but don't take that — it's five hundred micrograms twice a day, for five days. Stop if you get diarrhoea.
[SEG0041] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And if that doesn't agree with him?
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the colchicine doesn't suit him and he has to stop, naproxen five hundred milligrams twice a day with food instead, not both together. Keep the foot up, ease off the beer this weekend, and carry on with the blood pressure tablet as usual.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in two weeks so we can go through that blood result.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): And if the toe gets worse, or you feel feverish before then, come back sooner rather than waiting.

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): On the stairs, or if I'm hurrying for the bus. I'm alright sitting down.

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No pain in the chest.
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She went proper dizzy in Tesco last week. I thought she was going to keel over.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I didn't nearly faint. I was a bit light-headed standing in the queue, that's all. I don't know if I'd even call it dizzy, doctor.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any change in your hair? That crops up with this sort of thing.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, actually. It's coming out in the shower, and it looks thinner. A couple of months, maybe.
[SEG0025] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And it's on the pillow in the morning.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, a bit on the pillow. I noticed that as well.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are the periods still monthly, and is there pain?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Still about monthly. Crampy on the first day, nothing terrible. I don't know my exact cycle, mind.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any bleeding between periods, or after sex?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Neither of those.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bowels, or the waterworks — any change?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No, those are fine.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about medicines? Anything regular?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Iron. Ferrous sulphate, the two hundred milligram tablets. I was told once a day.
[SEG0035] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She takes it every morning with breakfast. I've watched her swallow it.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't. Not every day. Maybe two or three times a week, if I remember. I don't know, doctor, I'm rubbish with tablets.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): And when was the iron started?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): A few months ago. I can't remember the month. The other GP, I think.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, or to anything else?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I know of.
[SEG0041] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thyroid runs in our family. Her mum, my gran, was on thyroxine for years for an underactive thyroid. Gran's mother as well, I'm pretty sure.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, my mum was. Further back than that, I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any operations, or illnesses of your own?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): No operations. Nothing else, really. Touch wood.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or drink?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Never smoked. A glass of wine at the weekend, that's about it. I do three days in the school office, and the stairs there finish me off.
[SEG0047] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We were stuck on the ring road for forty minutes, by the way. Total gridlock. Cricket was on the radio, England folding again before lunch. I don't know why I listen.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): I caught some of that innings in the car. Woeful middle order. At least the weather's held, not like that washout last Thursday.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): My grandson had a game on Saturday too, under-elevens. More interested in the orange squash and the biscuits than the bowling, bless him.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sounds about right for that age. On examination you're pale, the inner eyelids especially. Pulse is ninety-six, blood pressure one hundred and eighteen over seventy-four. Chest is clear, heart sounds are normal, and there's no murmur.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thinking it through, my working idea is iron deficiency from the heavy periods — the tiredness, the breathlessness when you exert yourself, the hair — though I won't call that definite until the bloods are back. An underactive thyroid is possible as well, with your mum's history, so I'm keeping that in the mix.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll send you for bloods today: a full blood count, a ferritin, and thyroid function. If the bleeding carries on like this, or the count comes back badly down, we might arrange a pelvic ultrasound. I'm not booking that today.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do keep up the iron, the two hundred milligrams every day rather than now and then. Have it with orange juice, and not with tea, because tea blocks it. If it upsets your stomach, say so and we can change the preparation.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks and we'll go through the results together. If you're much more breathless before then, or you're soaking through faster, don't wait for that — ring us or come back.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright. I don't know if I'll remember all of that, doctor.
[SEG0056] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll write the iron bit down for her so it actually happens.
